bio.en: Jeremy Henrickson is Senior Vice President of Product at Rippling, where he leads product and design, and was previously Chief Product Officer at Coinbase, where he oversaw 10x growth of the product and engineering orgs during a turbulent crypto period.
bio.zh: Jeremy Henrickson 是 Rippling 的产品高级副总裁，领导产品与设计团队，此前曾任 Coinbase 首席产品官，在加密市场剧烈波动的时期带领产品与工程组织实现了 10 倍增长。

summary.en: Jeremy shares lessons on maintaining velocity at scale and creating a culture of fast decision-making, emphasizing that product leaders should go deep on the hardest problems alongside their teams rather than directing from above. He explains why relying on frameworks can hurt, why he often favors designing for the most complex use cases first over MVPs, what to look for when interviewing PMs, and how to become a true domain expert. The episode is a grounded playbook for product leaders operating at large, complex organizations.
summary.zh: Jeremy 分享了在规模化下保持速度、建立快速决策文化的经验，强调产品领导者应当深入最棘手的问题、与团队并肩作战，而非高高在上发号施令。他解释了为何依赖框架反而有害、为何他常主张先为最复杂的用例做设计而非先做 MVP、面试 PM 时看什么，以及如何成为真正的领域专家。这期节目是在大型复杂组织中运作的产品领导者的踏实手册。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: It's very, very tempting to float up here as a leader and say, "Hey, you take that hill over there. You guys do this over here." When in fact, where you really learn where the challenges are, or the problems or the successes is by just being there with the people in the trenches on one of the things, whichever one seems hardest or most complicated. And so I try to do that as often as I can, and I found that I always learn a lot by going through that detailed exercise.
turns.zh: 身为领导者，真心很想站在高处发号施令：“嘿，你去占领那边的山头；你们负责这边的行动。”但实际上，要想真正了解挑战所在、问题症结或成功秘诀，最有效的办法就是亲自深入基层，参与最困难、最复杂的工作。因此，我尽可能多地参与一线工作，发现通过这种深入实践，总能收获宝贵的经验。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me. I'm excited to be here.

turns.en: So I've heard nothing but amazing things about you and I'm excited to learn from what you've learned from your experience at Rippling, at Coinbase, and all of the products and teams that you've built. And so thank you again for being here.
turns.zh: 我听说了很多关于您的精彩事迹，很期待从您在Rippling、Coinbase以及您所打造的其他产品和团队的经验中学习。再次感谢您的到来。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah, super happy to be here.
turns.zh: 是的，能来到这里我真的非常开心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I want to start with your time at Coinbase where you were chief product officer and you were chief product officer during maybe the craziest time in the crypto markets. It was I think 2016, 2018 when I was looking at the Bitcoin prices and it was like it went from a $1000 to $20,000 I think in a matter of months. So I'm curious, what was that experience like, and in particular, what was like leading a product team through that experience?
turns.zh: 首先，我想谈谈你在Coinbase的经历。你当时是首席产品官，而那正是加密货币市场最疯狂的时期。2016年和2018年左右，当时比特币价格从1000美元暴涨至2万美元，短短几个月间涨幅惊人。所以我很好奇，当时带领产品团队经历这段疯狂时期是怎样的体验？特别是如何在动荡中保持团队的专注力？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: The strongest memories for me are during 2017 where crypto, which had kind of been at its nadir in early 2016 and slowly started climbing out, just kind of took off and became a real thing in the public consciousness. And Coinbase, which at the time had an exchange just like on-ramp and off-ramp from fiat to crypto and back experienced over the course of 2017 40 x growth in usage.
turns.zh: 对我来说，最深刻的记忆是在2017年。当时，加密货币市场在2016年初触底后逐渐回升，最终在公众视野中彻底爆发。Coinbase当时只提供法币与加密货币的兑换服务，但2017年其用户量激增了40倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's like a dream come true for a lot of people.
turns.zh: 这对很多人来说简直是梦想成真。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: No, I mean it was both a dream and a nightmare and I was incredibly lucky to be working on it with a team of people that I could really trust and could stand shoulder-to-shoulder within the trenches. And it was a lot of learning about how you can rapidly scale systems over time and people like to trade crypto on Saturday mornings, so a lot of Saturday mornings just some new thing would break on the edges of the system and we need to get in there and work on it. And so it was just a lot of really incredible lessons about who you choose to work with and focus and making sure you have the right people in the room at the right time.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得这既是梦想也是噩梦。当时我非常幸运能与一群值得信赖的团队成员并肩作战。我们需要学习如何快速扩展系统，尤其是在周六早晨这种用户交易高峰期，系统边缘经常出现故障，必须及时修复。这让我深刻体会到，团队协作、专注力和人才储备至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So let's actually unpack a couple of those. So focus is really interesting and something people always talk about, but hard to actually do. I guess how did you keep the team focused? I imagine just everyone's getting rich all over the place in crypto.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我们来具体探讨一下。专注力确实是件难事，也是人们常谈却难做到的。你当时是如何保持团队专注的？我猜当时加密货币市场很多人都在暴富。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Huh.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Things are breaking all the time, like how did you maintain focus on your team?
turns.zh: 系统经常出故障，你们是如何保持团队专注的？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Well, the first thing is you don't talk about people getting rich. It's a very technical, you talk about like its customers, it's their money, and number one, it had to be secure. So there's a guy named Philip Barton, a friend of mine now, and he is just this amazing security leader at Coinbase, and he was able to always put these decisions that we were making extremely quickly in context and say, "Look, these are the kinds of decisions we can make and still have it be secure no matter how fast we need to move." And so security was always the number one thing. And then the second thing is focusing on both the kind of immediate nature of the issue. Hey, site is down or whatever, and resolving that, but also trying to set those in a context of where we need to go over the next six months. What are we actually shooting for? What do we believe the volumes are going to be? What's it going to take to have everything from a user experience to the deep back end of the product that what would actually work for them?
turns.zh: 首先，别谈论人们发财的事。这是技术层面的，要以客户和资金为核心。最重要的是安全性。Coinbase的菲利普·巴顿（Philip Barton）现在是我的好友，他是位杰出的安全负责人。他总能把我们快速做出的决策置于安全框架内，比如“无论速度多快，我们都能确保安全”。所以安全始终是首要任务。其次，要关注问题的紧迫性。比如网站宕机之类的，要及时解决，同时也要把这些问题放在未来六个月的战略框架中：我们的目标是什么？预期的交易量是多少？从用户体验到产品后端，哪些措施对用户最有效？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was maybe the biggest challenge as a product leader trying to keep people focused and everything on the rails as things were going 40 x?
turns.zh: 在产品负责人眼中，当业务量激增40倍时，保持团队专注和一切井井有条的最大挑战是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think the biggest challenge was that in crypto there's just so much uncertainty in general, simple questions like, is Ethereum going to be a thing, are the subject of debate. And no one actually at the time had an answer to that question. Lots of really strong opinions and so you have to be able to have those debates because lots is going on, but then you have to be able to come out of those conversations with a clear kind of company point of view that you're all shooting toward. And while there may still be differing points of views and debates that happen on the margins, you go full speed toward this answer until you decide to go full speed toward a different answer. And I thought we were pretty successful at that at Coinbase and it wasn't always easy.
turns.zh: 我认为最大的挑战在于，加密领域总体上存在着诸多不确定性。比如，"以太坊是否会继续存在"这样的简单问题都引发了激烈争论。当时根本没有人能给出确切答案。人们有很多强烈的观点，所以你必须参与这些讨论，因为事情进展迅速。但最终，你必须从这些对话中凝聚出一个清晰的公司发展方向，所有人都朝着这个目标努力。即便边缘领域仍存在分歧和争论，只要你全力朝着既定方向前进，直到决定转向新方向，这段旅程就是成功的。在Coinbase，我们在这方面做得不错，但过程并不容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe just a last question there.
turns.zh: 或许最后再问一个问题。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Living through a time like that, a lot of people are going through these periods of just intense work and it's like, holy moly, this isn't crazy stressful working, like incredibly long hours, but then you look back at those times, and end up being some most important meaningful periods of your career.
turns.zh: 经历这样的时期，很多人都会经历高强度工作期。当时觉得压力巨大——不是那种疯狂加班、长时间工作的压力，而是回首往事时才意识到，这些时期其实是职业生涯中最重要、最有意义的阶段。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess one is that, is that your experience too? And then two, I guess is there any advice for someone that's maybe going through something like that of just here's maybe the silver lining of being in a period like that?
turns.zh: 我想问两个问题：第一，这也是你的经历吗？第二，对正在经历类似时期的人，有什么建议吗？或许能从中发现一些积极意义？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: So it's hard, right? It wasn't always easy. I had a new daughter who had been born just a few months earlier, really tough to balance those things, but I've always loved the rate of learning. And so it is those experiences I feel that have most sort of accelerated my own personal growth and personal learnings because it's in the crucible of things being hard. And so I think when people are going through those times, it's nice to take a step back and talk with friends or whatever about what's really going on and setting it in the context of, hey, three, four or five years now from now when we look back on this, you realize, wow. A, we did something amazing with that time. And B, we learned a lot and we were able to take that with us into whatever we were doing next after that.
turns.zh: 这确实很艰难，对吧？当时并不容易。我女儿几个月前刚出生，平衡工作和家庭真的很困难，但我一直热爱快速学习的过程。正是在这些艰难的磨练中，我个人成长和学习速度最快。经历这些时期后，退后一步，和朋友聊聊当时的处境，再把它放在更长远的视角下看——比如三年、四年、五年后，回首往事，你会发现：哇，我们那段时间做了不起的事。我们学到了很多，并能将这些经验带入接下来的工作中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before our chat, I'd asked you what people ask you for advice most around, and you said that people often ask you for advice on how to maintain velocity at scale, which is something every founder and product leader is always striving to do. And so what have you learned and what do you tell people about maintaining and maybe even improving velocity as you scale?
turns.zh: 在我们的对话前，我问过你人们最常向你寻求什么建议，你说人们常问如何在规模化中保持发展速度。这是每个创始人和产品负责人始终在努力做的事情。那么你学到了什么，又会给人们什么建议来在规模化中保持甚至提升发展速度呢？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think there's a lot of different answers here, and I think a lot of them are very specific to the nature of the business that someone's in, like different businesses can maintain velocity in different ways. I think there's kind of a universal truth that you want small teams with clear missions. Right? If there's 300 people trying to work on one thing, the just sheer communication challenges, Dunbar's number, all of those things come into play and it's really, really hard to act quickly. And so having smaller groups of people breaking down what is always a very, very large problem into sufficiently small bits that small groups can attack wholeheartedly and minimize horizontal communication, I think is the first thing. I think the second thing is that to the extent it's like a technology problem. The more you can bake into a clear platform, it reduces the decision-making complexity for everyone who's working on the domain part of the problem. (00:10:09): And so a clear like a platform with a clear interface [inaudible 00:10:12] easy to use in all the ways that both engineers and product people want it to be easy to use, simplifies the space in which people have to think about these problems. And that's not always easy. Platforms are not, you can't just write a platform and hope it's going to work for the products. It's very much an iterative thing, but the more one can invest in that and have the right kinds of people who are capable of doing that sort of both systems thinking and product thinking simultaneously, I think is really important. The third thing, just from a leadership point of view is diving deep. Right? It's very, very tempting to float up here as a leader and say, "Hey, you take that hill over there, you guys do this over here." When in fact where you really learn where the challenges are or the problems or the successes is by just being there with the people in the trenches on one of the things, whichever one seems hardest or most complicated. (00:11:05): And so I try to do that as often as I can. And I found that I always learn a lot by going through that detailed exercise. And I think the last thing is it's just making sure that teams have the right distribution of experience and seniority. Sometimes you get a team started and the team is perhaps doing something that's zero-to-one and they're amazing at all this zero-to-one stuff. (00:11:28): And then two or three years later, those same people are trying to scale the product to millions of people and it turns out that A, they don't like that part of the job as much, and B, maybe they're not as good at it. So I think you [inaudible 00:11:40] constantly look at the team and make sure that a people are doing things that they love and if they're not like, Hey, we've tried this other thing instead and recalibrate the team and make sure the right kind of skill sets are there. And I found if you do all of those things and then have product leadership where we're saying this is what we need to do and very, very clear and precise on what needs to be done, then you can usually actually even accelerate over time because you bake more into this platform, it allows your engineers to do more with less, and that's always pretty amazing.
turns.zh: 我认为这里有很多不同的答案，其中很多都非常具体地针对某个行业的性质，比如不同的企业可以用不同的方式保持发展势头。我认为有一个普遍的真理，那就是你需要小团队和明确的使命。是吧？如果有300个人试图共同完成一件事，那么单纯的沟通挑战、达巴数量理论等因素都会产生影响，想要快速行动真的非常困难。因此，让较小的团队将一个始终非常庞大的问题分解成足够小的部分，让这些小组能够全心投入并最大限度地减少横向沟通，我认为这是首要之举。第二点是，如果这是一个技术问题。你越能将其整合到一个清晰的平台上，越能为负责该领域的团队成员减少决策复杂性。（00:10:09）：所以，一个清晰的平台，拥有明确的界面[00:10:12，听不清]，符合工程师和产品经理期望的易用性，能简化人们思考这些问题的环境。这并不容易。平台不是随便写出来就能适用于产品的，这是一个迭代的过程。但如果你能在这方面投入更多，并拥有能够同时兼顾系统思维和产品思维的合适人才，我认为这非常重要。第三点，从领导角度看，就是深入参与。是吧？作为领导者，很容易高高在上地说：“嘿，你们去攻克那边的难题，你们负责这边的工作。”但实际上，你真正了解挑战、问题或成功所在的方式，是亲身参与最困难或最复杂的工作。（00:11:05）：所以我尽可能多地这样做。我发现，通过这种详细的实践，我总能收获很多。最后一点是，确保团队拥有合理的经验和资历分布。有时你组建一个团队，他们可能正在做从0到1的创新工作，他们在这些创新领域表现出色。（00:11:28）：但两三年后，这些人试图将产品扩展到数百万用户，却发现他们A不喜欢这部分工作，B可能也不擅长此道。所以我认为你要不断审视团队，确保人们在做自己热爱的工作。如果不是这样，那就调整方向，重新调配团队，确保团队拥有合适的技能组合。我发现，如果你能做到这些，再加上明确的产品领导层，清楚地传达需要做什么，那么你通常就能随着时间推移不断加速发展，因为你能将更多功能整合到平台中，让工程师事半功倍，这总是令人惊叹的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let me dig into a couple of these. These are really great.
turns.zh: 好的，我来仔细看看这些内容。这些真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: [inaudible 00:12:10] please.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So with the small teams with clear missions, is there an example of that at Rippling or Coinbase where that was a really good example of this being true?
turns.zh: 关于小型团队和明确任务的问题，Rippling或Coinbase是否有这方面的成功案例可以借鉴？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: One example is maybe three years ago when I was just starting at the company, we decided that we needed to build a time and attendance product, lots of market demand for us and that we hadn't built it yet, something that many customers need. And so there were a bunch of ways we could have chosen to do that, but the way we did it was to say, look, let's find one engineer, really talented systems engineer who's actually capable of doing kind of product thinking and have Parker, CEO also spend time on it. And you start there and Sachit brought a few people on with him. (00:12:56): And those four people over the course of maybe nine months or so, built a time and attendance product. It was the only thing they were doing. They didn't have to worry about what was going on with our payroll product except to the extent they had to integrate with them a little bit. They didn't have to worry about what was going on with the benefits team or our IT products. They were monomaniacally focused on this one thing and then identifying the places where yes, you, there's connectivity to the rest of the suite, and that allowed them to move extremely quickly.
turns.zh: 举个例子，大概三年前我刚加入公司时，我们决定开发一款考勤管理产品。市场对这类产品的需求很大，但我们当时还没有推出过类似产品，许多客户都急需这类工具。当时我们可以采用多种方法来实现，但我们的做法是，找一位非常有才华的系统工程师，他既要具备产品思维能力，又要让首席执行官Parker亲自参与其中。然后，他们从头开始，Sachit带了几个人加入团队。（00:12:56）：在大约9个月的时间里，这四个人开发出了这款考勤管理产品。这是他们唯一专注的项目。他们无需操心薪资管理产品的情况，除非需要与其进行少量集成，也无需管福利团队或IT产品的事务。他们全身心投入到这项任务中，然后在必要时与其他部门进行对接，这使得他们的进展极为迅速。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much of that was Parker being on the team, helping them unblock everything versus being very small and focused?
turns.zh: 在这一过程中，Parker亲自参与团队，帮助他们解决难题，与团队规模小、专注度高相比，哪种方式更有效？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think it was mostly small and focused. Obviously, Parker can do things and unblock them in the way that only a CEO can and that helps. But the thing is at Rippling, like we've now replicated that a dozen times. That's our model for starting new things. And so it can't just be him unblocking things, though he does unblock things. It's more that this pattern of having these small groups be able to do things and then being able to have go to those people, whether you're Parker or somebody else in the company, and be able to say, Hey, how are things going? Or are we working on the right things? Or let's see the latest designs for that thing and comment on it. (00:14:05): All of those things can happen just at a much greater tempo than if you're trying to go three layers down into the org and do things. I think that's the other, maybe the key point here that everyone is exposed senior leadership, yes, we have a management structure because you have to, but that management structure does not interfere with the ability of anyone anywhere in the organization to look at what's actually happening. And that happens very directly.
turns.zh: 我认为主要还是团队规模小、专注度高很重要。显然，Parker作为CEO能够以独特方式化解难题，这确实很有帮助。但在Rippling，我们现在已经多次复制了这种模式。这是我们启动新项目的标准模式。因此，不能仅仅依赖他来解决问题——虽然他确实会介入——更重要的是，这种模式让小型团队能够独立开展工作，然后，无论是Parker还是公司其他高管，都能随时询问他们的进展、项目是否走在正确的道路上，或者查看最新设计并提出意见。（00:14:05）：所有这些交流都能以更高的效率进行，这比试图深入到公司三层级以下部门来推进工作要高效得多。我认为这也是另一个关键点，即所有人都能够接触到高层领导。当然，我们有必要的管理架构，但这种架构不会妨碍组织内任何成员直观了解实际情况。而这种交流是直接发生的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's talk about that model you just described. So what is that model? So this is how you approach new products, and I know within Rippling there's many, many products and features we're going to talk about this. And you're saying that you have kind of an approach to adding a new business unit essentially, or a new product feature.
turns.zh: 那让我们来谈谈你刚才描述的模式。那么这种模式到底是什么？这是你们开发新产品的方法，我知道Rippling有很多新产品和功能，我们接下来要讨论这个。你们是在说如何添加一个新的业务部门，或者一个新的产品功能。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is that model roughly?
turns.zh: 这种模式大致是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah, so the model's quite simple. In the vast majority of cases, we realize we need to build something and we have the one-page view of what that is. And usually, we're lucky enough that the things we're building sort of exist in some form in the industry today, not in the differentiated way that we can build it, but time and attendance is an example. That's a well-known thing in the industry. There's whole companies that do only that, right? So we start there, we find a single engineer who is extremely entrepreneurial, understands what it means to operate at tempo, understands what it means to make decisions with low information, understands how to work very, very quickly with a design partner. (00:15:22): So we have a design partner and we say, "Look, come into Rippling, spend a few months getting to know the platform first of all. So go work on this other team, understand what's easy for them, what's hard for them, how the platform works, how other products have been built on top of this. Go talk with other people who founded products here and understand what their experience is so that you can learn from and iterate on it, get an opinion about your product, and then start building it." (00:15:48): And during this intervening time, they're also recruiting a team of usually 2, 3, 4 other engineers who kind of have that same zero-to-one mentality and they start building. And usually over the course of six to nine months, we can get a product from a blank sheet of paper to something that is launched or at least that we're using internally when we dogfood our stuff really heavily. And then it grows from there. And then sometimes when you launch one of these products, you get close to launch, you realize, hey, actually a team of five or six people can handle this product ad nauseam. Sometimes you have to bump it up. It's like, okay, this thing's about to go to production, there's all these other things to do, the team needs now needs to go from 4 to 15 or something like that. Really depends on the product, but that's the general life cycle and then you keep growing and scaling it.
turns.zh: 是的，这个模式其实挺简单的。在绝大多数情况下，我们意识到需要开发某个产品时，往往只有一个初步的构想。通常，我们很幸运能找到现成的行业解决方案，虽然不一定完全符合我们的需求，但时间考勤就是一个例子。这个功能在业界已经很成熟，甚至有专门的公司只做这项业务。（00:15:22）所以我们从这里入手，找一位极具创业精神的工程师，他要理解快速迭代的节奏，掌握低信息量决策的技巧，还能与设计伙伴高效协作。（00:15:48）在过渡阶段，我们会招募2到4名具备类似零到一思维的工程师，组成团队开始开发。通常在6到9个月内，我们就能将一个白纸阶段的产品推向市场，或者至少在内部大量使用。之后，产品会不断迭代优化。有时产品上线前夕，我们会发现只需5到6人就能维持运作，于是团队规模随即扩容至15人左右。这完全取决于产品特性，但整体生命周期大致如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is fascinating. So just so I understand, you find a founder type to take the lead on a new idea and do you recruit them internally or you sometimes find them externally just to focus on this product?
turns.zh: 这真是太有趣了。那么我理解的是，你们会寻找有创业精神的创始人来主导新项目，那么这些创始人是内部招募还是外部引进呢？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Both.
turns.zh: 两者都有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有意思。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Both.
turns.zh: 两者都有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then you find a design partner for them to work with to figure out what exactly needs to be built. And is it idea pick one design partner or you try to encourage a few?
turns.zh: 好的。然后你们会为他们寻找设计合作伙伴，帮助他们明确产品需求。是选定一个设计合作伙伴，还是会邀请多个团队参与？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Usually, it's one. So there's a designer, so we have a design-
turns.zh: 通常会选定一个。就是找一位设计师，我们有专门的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, design partner, meaning a designer, not a company that is like their partner in design.
turns.zh: 哦，设计合作伙伴，指的是设计师个人，而不是某家设计公司作为合作伙伴。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Oh, no, no, no. Literally, somebody who knows Rippling's products, knows our component library, knows all of that stuff and is skilled and doing UX and interaction and visual design.
turns.zh: 哦，不不不。不，是指熟悉Rippling产品、了解我们的组件库、具备交互设计和视觉设计能力的专业设计师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay, design. Okay, cool. And then they basically with maybe a couple engineers, just that's the team that initiates a new product line and then launches it, and then as it scales, it maybe grows the team, maybe not.
turns.zh: 明白了。好的，设计环节。嗯，挺酷的。然后他们可能带着几个工程师，组建一个团队，启动新产品线并推向市场，之后根据发展情况扩容团队。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yep, that's right. And it's pretty ad hoc, but every couple of weeks or something like that, they're meeting with me or with Parker or whichever one of us is the DRI on it and giving feedback on the designs, having a critical life or like "Oh man, if I were using this as a admin, a small company or an admin at a large company, how would I feel about this? Would this interface work for me?" And so we were pressure testing it throughout that cycle and trying to get the balance of speed and comprehensiveness, right.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。这过程相当临时化，但每隔几周左右，他们就会和我或帕克，或者我们中负责该项目的DRO（直接责任人）开会，针对设计方案提出反馈，比如“天啊，如果我是管理员、一家小公司或大公司的管理层，我会怎么看待这个界面？这个界面能满足我的需求吗？”在整个开发周期中，我们不断进行压力测试，努力平衡速度与全面性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me you're also, I hear not a big fan of MVPs that you building products to further point. Is that true? And then if so, how do you think about the initial version of a product?
turns.zh: 这让我想起，你之前还说过不喜欢用来快速验证产品的MVP（最小可行产品）。是这样吗？如果是这样，你如何看待产品的初始版本？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: First of all, I don't want to knock on MVPs. I think MVPs have their place extremely useful, particularly if you're literally the zero-to-one company that's never done anything before and you don't have clear market validation. I think in our case specifically for Rippling, a minimum viable product would do a disservice to both our customers and to the very team that was building it. And the reason I believe that is that when you design a minimum viable product, you're optimizing for speed. And in that set of optimizations, you are minimizing the deeper product thinking about what can fully differentiate our product based on not only existing kind of capabilities within our products and platform, but based on what it ought to do in the future. (00:19:03): And so it sort of limits product creativity, but worse, it leads to building the wrong thing technically, right? So if you're only thinking through the simple cases and you're an engineer and no one's pushing you on saying, "Wait, what about that healthcare hospital administration case where it's mission-critical life," then you're going to make a different set of as architectural assumptions, and then you're going to build on those and you're going to build on those for six months, nine months a year, and you'll have dozens or 100s of assumptions built on top of those. (00:19:38): And it's extremely difficult to unwind those decisions once you've built them into the product. And therefore we believe very deeply it's like, sure, understand those simple cases. Understand if you're a two-person company, you don't need all of these other things. And what is the product going to look like for you to approach it but also understand what it would mean to have 10,000 people globally around the world with this ridiculously hard use case? What's the model that would support that? And let's make sure that as we're doing the technical and product design for this thing, that it accommodates that view, even if we're not going to support it in the first version, even if we make the product decision to say, "Look, we actually don't need to handle that case right now." You still build the product in a way that's not going to prevent you from getting there in the future. And does that take a little more time? Sure, yeah. But does it save you time in the long run? Absolutely. Right. And so that's our approach.
turns.zh: 首先，我不想贬低MVP的价值。我认为MVP在某些情况下非常有用，特别是对于从零到一的初创公司，如果你之前从未涉足相关领域且缺乏市场验证的话。在Rippling的案例中，最小可行产品对我们的客户和开发团队都弊大于利。原因在于，当你设计最小可行产品时，会优先优化速度。在这种优化过程中，人们会尽量减少对产品的深层思考——不仅要考虑现有产品和平台的功能，还要展望未来可能的应用场景。这会限制产品的创造力，更糟糕的是，可能导致技术层面错误的决策。（00:19:03）比如，如果你只考虑简单场景，而工程师又没有人提醒你，“等等，医疗医院管理这种关键任务场景呢？”那么你可能会做出错误的架构假设，并在接下来的六个月、九个月、一年里基于这些假设持续开发，最终积累数十个甚至上百个错误假设。（00:19:38）而这些决策一旦融入产品，就很难再回头。因此，我们坚信，尽管理解简单场景很重要，理解两人的小公司不需要所有这些功能也很重要，但也要思考全球1万人面临这种极端复杂场景时会怎样？支持这种场景的商业模式是什么？在进行技术和产品设计时，要确保产品架构能适应未来需求。即使第一版不支持这些功能，也要确保产品设计能为未来铺路。这会多花点时间吗？当然。但从长远来看，这样做能节省时间吗？绝对能。对，这就是我们的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that comes to mind of a product you build at Rippling or Coinbase of just, it could have been this really simple MVP and then ended up being like, no, we did the right thing by building it further along the spectrum.
turns.zh: 你能举个例子说明Rippling或Coinbase开发的产品原本可能是简单的MVP，但最终因为深入开发而取得成功吗？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah. So I think a great example of this at Rippling is our global payroll product. We could have said, "Hey, look, we just need to support this one country. We need to support, whatever, the UK," let's say. So we're going to copy all of our US stuff, just replicate it and change all the things to be UK-like. That would've been the fastest thing to do to dramatically oversimplify, but that's not what we did. What we did is we said, look, we need to launch a six countries and these are six super different countries that we want to look at. And they're going to have different requirements from an HRIS standpoint, from an employer of record standpoint, from how you pay global contractors, from how payroll works, and we're going to make a system that works for those countries. And there's lots of downstream implications for that. (00:21:39): But what it means is that now our global payroll system, adding a country is, it's not easy, but it's a lot easier than it would've been if you had to continue to stamp out and replicate and then of course maintain all of these things that have very little underlying connectivity. And instead, what we have is 80% of the system is baked into our global payroll platform, and then the 20% is country-specific. And most of that specificity can be handled not by engineers who are very, very expensive to change things that are local specific, but instead can be configured by somebody that's in compliance, by somebody that's in legal that needs to get the right documents into the system. And all of that stuff can be handled by the system, which allows us to move much faster sort of going forward.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我认为Rippling的一个很好的例子就是我们的全球薪资管理产品。我们本可以说,"嘿，看，我们只需要支持这个国家。就支持英国吧,"比如说。这样做的话，我们只需复制美国的所有功能，稍作调整以适应英国的需求。但这显然是最简单粗暴的办法，但这不是我们选择的路径。我们当时的思路是，我们需要在六个国家上线服务，而这六个国家有着截然不同的需求——从人力资源信息系统（HRIS）的角度，从雇主身份认证的角度，从全球合同工薪资支付方式，到薪资管理流程等各个方面。我们要开发一个能适配这些国家的系统。这背后有着诸多深远的影响。（00:21:39）但这意味着现在我们的全球薪资管理系统，增加一个国家的难度固然不小，但比起必须不断重复开发、然后还要维护那些几乎没有底层关联性的功能要容易得多了。相反，我们的系统中，80%的功能都已内置于全球薪资管理平台，而剩下的20%则针对特定国家的需求。这些特定需求大多无需由昂贵的工程师团队去更改，而是可以由合规人员或法律团队来配置——他们只需将正确的文件导入系统即可。所有这些操作都可以通过系统完成，这让我们能够更快地推进后续工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've heard you describe this kind of idea as you encourage teams to design for the most complex use case first.
turns.zh: 我听你描述过这种理念，即你鼓励团队先为最复杂的用例进行设计。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that kind of the instruction you give these teams?
turns.zh: 这是你给这些团队的指导方针吗？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: 100%, many times. And so it's one of these things that until you're here, it's a really difficult thing to kind of grok because A, it's so counterculture to what the background that most people have come from. It's like, no, no, no, don't think about all those things. Just zoom in on this one case, use it as a wedge, and then grow from there. And this is one of the reasons that we have people, especially new people in these kind of founding roles, come in and spend a few months just absorbing the culture to really learn these lessons. And it's one reason that we're extremely high touch with kind of new products in their infancy to make sure that we just don't fall into that trap, right? Especially because simultaneously with doing this, we're like, "Hey, but we need to ship this as fast as possible." Right? And so you want to get the balance of those two things right.
turns.zh: 百分之百是，很多次都是这样。这是其中一个难点，因为这与大多数人的背景文化相悖。人们总会说，别想那么多，就专注于这个案例，以此为切入点，然后再逐步扩展。这也是为什么我们让新加入的创始团队成员花几个月时间沉浸在公司文化中，真正领会这些理念的原因之一。这也是为什么我们对初期产品保持高度关注，确保不重蹈覆辙。尤其是当我们同时要快速上线产品时，就更需要平衡好这两者之间的关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when I think about Rippling, I think of you got the culture is to do things the hard way and the right way. And an element of that is there's this concept that I've heard that Rippling is this compound startup? What does that term mean? And then how does that approach impact the way you build product and organize teams and all the things you were just talking about of MVPs and build new products?
turns.zh: 所以当我想到Rippling时，我觉得你们的文化是倾向于用困难但正确的方式做事的。其中一个理念是，Rippling是一家复合型初创公司？这个术语是什么意思？那这种方法又如何影响你们的产品开发、团队组织，以及你刚才提到的MVP和新产品开发呢？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: The idea of a compound startup for us is that we're basically a lot of businesses that all work together. If you think about the products we offer, we have payroll, well, there's entire companies built just on payroll, insurance, and benefits, entire companies. That's our entire life. In fact, a fragment of benefits is the entire life cycle of a whole company. Our IT products, device management, and identity management, time and attendance, each of these things are industries into themselves with multi-billion dollar companies serving each of them. The insight Parker had before he founded the company was actually the result you get that when you have that is that there's all this data that gets replicated and copied and as impossible to keep in sync everywhere. The right answer is to have a single system of record, one place, one database where all of that information is resident so that each of these downstream systems can always have the right data at the right time. (00:24:34): And then you can build on top of that things like workflow and reporting and analytics and permissioning and all these kinds of underlying capabilities. So the idea of a compound startup is all of these different businesses benefit from being built on top of one platform. The activation energy for that is extremely high. So before my time at the company, Parker, Prasanna, the technical founder, and others, built all of the first versions of all these products and it was a minor miracle, they were able to do that. But having done it, we then had that platform and we could continue to build new verticals and new startups on top of that foundation.
turns.zh: 对我而言，复合型初创公司的理念在于，我们本质上是众多相互协作的业务单元。如果你审视我们提供的产品——比如薪资管理，实际上有整家公司专注于薪资、保险和福利业务，规模庞大。这正是我们的核心业务。事实上，福利管理这一环节就涵盖了一家完整公司的全生命周期。我们的IT产品、设备管理、身份管理、考勤管理等，每一项都是独立的行业，都有数十亿美元规模的公司为其提供服务。帕克在创立公司前提出的洞察，实质上是当你整合所有数据时，会发现数据存在重复和冗余，难以实现全局同步。正确的解决方案是建立单一的数据库系统，将所有信息统一存储在一个地方，这样下游系统就能在恰当的时间获取准确的数据。（00:24:34）在此基础上，再开发工作流、报告、分析、权限管理等底层功能。因此，复合型初创公司的核心理念是，让不同业务单元共用一个平台获益。实现这一目标的技术门槛极高。在我加入公司之前，帕克、技术联合创始人普拉萨纳等人完成了所有产品的初版开发，这堪称奇迹。但一旦搭建起平台，我们就能在此基础上持续开拓新领域、孵化新公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on something that comes up a number of times in this podcast, which is the importance of differentiation. And it feels like this is the differentiator for Rippling. It's not going to be just a better one of these vertical solutions like the main differentiators, we're going to do it all and everything's going to be so much better because it's all in one platform. Is that kind of where the original idea came from or is there a different way to think about that?
turns.zh: 这与播客中多次提及的差异化策略息息相关。似乎这正是Rippling的核心竞争力。与主要竞争对手专注于某个垂直领域不同，Rippling志在整合所有业务，并通过统一平台实现质的飞跃。这是否就是最初构想的核心逻辑？还是有更深层的解读角度？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's right. So I mean, the fundamental contention is having a single system of record is better for many, many, many reasons, right? The most simple of which is there's a single source of truth and all of these other products can rely on it. But also, unless you start without assumption of everything being in a single system of record, there's a bunch of other things you can't do. You can't build out a, I don't know, a permissioning system that looks at the various attributes across all of these products. You now suddenly have to do an integration and each of these products talks different languages. You can't do simple things, build a product and say, who is this person's manager? Most products, you can't do that. Most products you find some system of truth, export everybody's name and email address and a spreadsheet, have another email address or another name, maybe an employee ID of who that person reports to and upload that to another system, which by the way is immediately out of date because organizational structures change all the time. (00:26:35): Whereas with Rippling, it's always correct. We are the system of record. So all of our products, they're like, "Hey, who's that person's manager." And the system immediately knows. And that's a very, very simple example of something that you can only do if you start with solve it to come back to an earlier point, like solve the most complex use case first, solve the fact that this data all needs to be in the same place. And so our ability to differentiate boils down to that one fundamental decision, which just allows us to do things that are literally impossible for any other company to do.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得这没错。所以我的意思是，出于诸多原因，采用单一的数据记录系统要好得多，对吧？最简单的一点是，数据有单一的真实来源，所有其他产品都可以依赖它。但除非你从一开始就假设所有数据都存储在单一的数据记录系统中，否则很多事情都无法实现。比如，你无法构建一个权限管理系统，该系统需要查看所有产品中的各种属性。现在你突然需要进行集成，而每个产品都使用不同的语言。有些简单的事情，比如构建一个产品并询问“这个人的上司是谁？”大多数产品都做不到这一点。大多数产品会先找到某个数据源，将所有人的姓名和邮箱导出到电子表格中，然后再查找其他邮箱或姓名，或许还有员工ID，接着将这些信息上传到另一个系统，但这些信息很快就会过时，因为组织架构总是在不断变化。

（00:26:35）：而Rippling始终是正确的。我们就是数据记录系统。因此，我们所有的产品都会问“这个人的上司是谁？”系统会立即给出答案。这只是一个非常简单的例子，说明只有从一开始就以解决问题为导向才能做到这一点——比如先解决最复杂的用例，再解决所有数据必须存储在同一位置的问题。我们的竞争力归根结底取决于这一关键决策，它让我们能够做到其他公司根本无法做到的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What would you say is one of the most unique things about Ripplings culture that maybe you haven't mentioned yet?
turns.zh: 你认为Ripplings文化中最独特的方面之一是什么？也许你还没有提及过？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I would say it's fundamental, speed of execution. I think in speed of decision-making. It's the thing that is probably the hardest to explain to people before they're here. It's hard to understand until you experience it. It's like let's not schedule a meeting for next week or tomorrow or later today. We're in the middle of a meeting, we need to make a decision. Let's either make the decision or if we can't, let's Slack call in the person that we need in order to make that decision. And we'll be done with the decision today. (00:27:44): And like sure there are irreversible decisions you can't make that way, but for the most part, we really value the tempo of decision-making and the speed of response. And no company I've been at any scale, 5 people, 5,000 people, has ever operated at the tempo this one does. And I think that our ability to continue to operate at that tempo, which is partly due to the fact that we are a compound startup and have these small teams independently operating teams and all the rest of that is a really differentiating thing about the culture of the company.
turns.zh: 我认为是执行速度的根本重要性。我认为这也是最难向新人解释的部分。除非亲身经历，否则很难理解。比如，我们不会把会议安排到下周、明天或者今天晚些时候。我们正在开会，需要做决定。 either make the decision or if we can't, let's Slack call in the person that we need in order to make that decision. And we'll be done with the decision today. (00:27:44): 当然，有些不可逆转的决定不能这样做，但大多数情况下，我们非常重视决策的节奏和响应速度。在我接触过的任何规模的公司——无论是5人、5000人——都没有达到我们这样的节奏。我认为我们能够持续保持这种节奏的能力（部分原因在于我们是一家复合型初创公司，拥有独立运作的小团队等），是公司文化中真正与众不同的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm reading Kevin Kelly's new book where I don't know if you've seen his new book. It's all these little tidbits of advice and one of his pieces of advice is that usually the best time to do something is right now. And that feels like that resonates with the way you all think. I'm curious just how you create that culture and ability to make decisions fast. Is it purely top-down founder, this is how they behave, or is there something else that you found as effective to create this culture of moving fast, making decisions really quickly?
turns.zh: 我正在读凯文·凯利的新书，不知道你们是否读过这本书。书中有很多小贴士，其中一条建议是，通常做事的最佳时机就是当下。这感觉和你们的思维方式很契合。我很好奇，你们是如何营造这种文化，培养快速决策的能力的？是完全自上而下的创始人行为模式，还是有其他有效的方法来打造这种快速行动、快速决策的文化？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Obviously, a huge piece of this is Parker himself. It's an attribute of his personality, he likes making decisions quickly, and it's also a deliberate strategic decision on his part to have a company that makes decisions quickly. And so he models this constantly, right, in Slack, in conversations in person, and in every way possible. And there's an expectation throughout the company. If you kind of look at our leadership principles, this ability to make decisions quickly is something that kind of everybody promulgates. But also I think there's a number of things we've done to bake it in the way that we even do say quarterly planning. And the fact that there's this timeline for decision-making that doesn't leave a lot of room in the way that we expect people to know their domains, especially in product, right? (00:29:29): In product, you don't own little feature, you own your product and you're expected to be the world's foremost expert in it. And if you are, what that means is instead of having to come back to people three days later with an answer, just off the top of your head, you can be like, "Yes, this is what I think I should do about that or give me 30 minutes, look something up and I can tell you what we need to do about that." And so all of those things in combination just yield an environment in which these decisions happen very quickly.
turns.zh: 显然，帕克本人是关键因素。这既是他个性的体现——他喜欢快速决策，也是他有意为之的战略决策，打造一个能快速决策的公司。他不断以身作则，无论是在Slack上、面对面交流，还是通过各种方式，都在传递这种文化。整个公司都对此有期望。如果看我们的领导原则，快速决策能力是每个人都要践行的。此外，我们还采取了多种措施来固化这种文化，比如季度规划。这种决策时间表不给人太多回旋余地——我们期望每个人都能深耕自己的领域，尤其是在产品部门。（00:29:29）在产品部门，你不负责某个小功能，而是要对整个产品负责，必须成为该领域的顶级专家。如果你能做到这一点，当别人三天后向你要答案时，你就能脱口而出：“是的，我认为应该这么做。”或者说：“给我30分钟查一下资料，我就能告诉你该怎么做。”所有这些因素共同营造了一个快速决策的环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about quarterly planning and you're saying that there's like, here's the timelines we need to make decisions on these dates, and there's a culture of just we stay firm to that. And if you don't, then we're going to move on.
turns.zh: 你提到季度规划，意思是设定了特定日期必须做出决策，并且形成了一种坚守这些时间节点的文化。如果没做到，项目就会继续推进。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: That's right. And it's shocking to people when we actually move on, right, that haven't been here yet. It's like, no, no, that date passed. You don't get to retroactively make everybody react to the fact that you didn't operate quickly enough, right? And it's not a hostile thing, it's just a, people just have to get used to. It's a deep cultural principle. And the fact that everyone stands behind it just means it's gets reinforced on its own, out of its own gravity.
turns.zh: 没错。当新人加入公司，发现我们真的会直接推进时，他们会很惊讶。这就像在说，‘不行，不行，这个日期已经过了。你不能事后要求大家因为你决策不够快而重新反应。’这不是恶意，而是大家需要适应。这是深层的文化原则。每个人都支持它，就意味着它会自然强化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have internal values that you've kind of outlined that are a part of this? Or is that not something that you find super valuable?
turns.zh: 你们有明确的内部价值观作为这一文化的支撑吗？还是说你们不认为这很重要？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: No, actually I find them quite valuable. And actually our COO, Matt MacInnis, who joined the company about a year before I did, he has been the one to really drive this and you go to, I can't remember this specific URL, but on Rippling there's a search Rippling leadership principles. There they are. And they are really true to the culture of the company. The way we came up with them was to us a couple years ago, to introspect and to what actually made people successful at the company? Like who's successful, why are they successful? Why do they enjoy being here? Or alternatively the opposite, like why people not worked out, why do some people not enjoy it here? And those are the things that are differentiating and those are the things that we wrote down.
turns.zh: 事实上，我认为它们非常有价值。我们的首席运营官马特·麦金尼斯（Matt MacInnis）大约在我加入公司前一年加入了公司，他是真正推动这一进程的人。你可以去Rippling平台，搜索“Rippling领导力原则”，就能找到它们。这些原则与公司的文化非常契合。几年前，我们开始反思，究竟是什么让员工在公司取得成功？比如，谁是成功者？他们为什么能成功？他们为什么喜欢在这里工作？反之，哪些人不适应公司环境？为什么有些人不喜欢在这里工作？这些都是与众不同的关键要素，也是我们总结出的核心价值观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you hiring or on the flip side, are you looking for a new opportunity? Well, either way, check out lennysjobs.com/talent. If you're a hiring manager, you can sign up and get access to hundreds of hand-curated people who are open to new opportunities. Thousands of people apply to join this collective. And I personally review and accept just about 10% of them. You won't find a better place to hire product managers and growth leaders. Join almost a 100 other companies who are actively hiring through this collective. And if you're looking around for a newer opportunity actively or passively join the collective, it's free. You can be anonymous and you can even hide yourself from specific companies. You can also leave any time and you'll only hear from companies that you want to hear from. Check out lennysjobs.com/talent. For someone listening that's like, we need to move faster. And everyone always feels this, we need to move faster, we make decisions faster. What piece of advice would you give someone for helping them do this at their company?
turns.zh:
你是在招聘新员工，还是在寻找新的职业机会？无论哪种情况，欢迎访问l越来越多的公司通过这个平台积极招聘人才。数千人申请加入这个集体，而我亲自筛选并接纳其中约10%的候选人。你找不到比这里更适合招聘产品经理和增长团队负责人的平台了。加入近100家正在通过这个平台积极招聘的公司吧。如果你正在主动或被动寻找新的机会加入这个集体，完全免费。你可以匿名注册，甚至隐藏自己的身份，随时退出，只接收感兴趣公司的消息。欢迎访问lennysjobs.com/talent。  

对于那些急于行动的人，我会建议：我们需要更快地行动。每个人都迫切希望能更快地做决策。但你会如何帮助公司里的某个人实现这一目标呢？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think it's really context-dependent, but I think it starts with whoever is in the role of making the top-level product decisions of them being one extremely clear about what those priorities are and more importantly, extremely clear about what all the priorities aren't. Right? There are so many things that could be important or people can make the case for being important or whatever that are fundamentally distracting from the core mission of getting something done. (00:32:55): But secondly, for that person to go all the way to ground on it, we have one of the leadership principles is go and see. Right? So to look at the thing and then walk all the way to ground and talk with the engineer who's writing the code on the thing. Because inevitably this top-level communication is insufficient to get to the detail of what matters and doesn't matter. And you don't have to do that everywhere, but if you do it in enough places, what it does is it creates a clear expectation of that kind of clarity across the board and forces everyone to up their game a little bit and just helps people understand what the expectation is. Right? And I think in the absence of those sort of clear expectations, it's difficult for people to perform at their best. Right? And so we try to do that pretty frequently.
turns.zh: 我认为这取决于具体情况，但首先，负责制定顶层产品决策的人必须对这些优先事项有清晰的认识，更重要的是，对所有不重要的优先事项也要有清晰的认识。毕竟，太多看似重要或值得争取的东西，最终只会分散我们完成核心任务的注意力。（00:32:55）其次，要让决策者真正深入基层。我们有条领导原则叫“实地考察”。比如，亲自去看看某个项目，再去和写代码的工程师交流。因为顶层沟通往往无法触及细节，而这些细节决定着哪些重要，哪些不重要。当然，不必每个环节都如此，但在足够多的环节中践行这一原则，能在全公司范围内建立清晰的期望，促使每个人提升自身能力，让大家明白什么是被期待的。在缺乏这种清晰期望的情况下，员工很难发挥出最佳水平。因此，我们经常这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I definitely want to spend more time on this, but before we get there, so go and see. I love that. And that actually has come up recently on a number of podcasts, just the importance of people continuing to ask questions and going to the end of what's possible. Recent story was IO talking about building the cash card and going to the warehouse and watching the printings of the cards and things like that.
turns.zh: 好的。我确实想多花些时间在这上面，但在深入探讨之前，先去看看吧。我很欣赏这一点。事实上，最近多个播客节目都谈到了这个话题——强调人们持续提问、探索可能性边界的重要性。最近IO的播客就讲述了他们如何打造现金卡，然后亲自到仓库观看卡片打印等过程。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess first of all, do you have a sense of where that came from and why that ended up being so important to y'all? And then two is there an example of you doing that or someone you've seen do that and that leading to something really important?
turns.zh: 首先，你能否讲讲这源自何处？为什么它对你们如此重要？其次，你或身边的人有没有这样的例子，通过这种方式发现了重要价值？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: In the early days of our global efforts, when we were first trying to figure out what global payroll was, it was really tempting to say, "Oh, well we're going to go into the UK and that's going to be relatively similar to what we're doing in the US." But our kind of head of payroll went in and said, actually, here are the ways in which we knew it was going to be different, but here are the ways in which we didn't anticipate that it was going to be different, which made us realize that we had to completely alter our approach for how we think about learning about each of these countries and going into them and having a fulsome experience. (00:34:50): And that then backs into things like, well, every country does tax filings, every country does them slightly differently, but how are we going to build a tax filing system that's going to allow us to satisfy the needs of every country in which we're going to run payroll? And it was only through that very early on deep look at how one country was actually operating and then doing the same thing with the next country that we were able to set in motion, all of those things. It's not like we knew all the answers at that point, but it allowed us at a much earlier stage to put in motion a bunch of stuff that we need to do that then got subsequently much more clarified and much more precise over time.
turns.zh:
在我们全球化进程的初期，当我们试图理解全球薪资管理的本质时，很自然地会想：“哦，我们先去英国市场，那里应该和美国很相似。”但我们的薪资主管深入研究后指出，虽然我们预料到会有差异，但还有些意料之外的挑战。这让我们意识到，要想深入了解各国市场、顺利开展业务，必须彻底调整思路。
（00:34:50）：这就引出了关键问题：每个国家都征收税款，但各国政策差异巨大。如何构建一个能满足全球多国税务合规需求的系统？正是通过这种早期深入研究某个国家的税务体系，再将经验复用到其他国家，我们才得以推动整个进程。当时我们并不知道所有答案，但这让我们在早期就启动了关键工作，随后随着时间推移，这些工作得到了不断完善和精细化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so the leader of that team basically just went and studied the tax laws of each-
turns.zh: 所以那个团队的负责人基本上就是去研究每个国家的税法——

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... country.
turns.zh: ……每个国家的税法。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: That's right, went all the way to ground. It's like, okay, let's go and open up the big old, I mean, it's online these days, the big old textbook and look like it's, or you're in the United States, it's like you have to go look at Ohio or Pennsylvania, which have all these little local city or county based taxes. And it's incredibly instructive to look at just a few of those and think, wow, how do I think about configuring these change unannounced? Some city administrator or the city legislature, whatever they call them, they decide to change the tax rate. Well, how are we going to know about that? How are we going to change it? How are we going to change it so it's effective at the right time? (00:36:14): And you don't think about those things until you've gone all the way to ground and looked at how these things are actually worked, how they're communicated, and how they're thought through. And I think the same thing is true of every aspect of every product in different ways. Right? It might be a technical thing, it might be a design thing, it might be a compliance or a regulatory or a governmental thing, but whatever it is, that detail always exists. And unless you're getting down there and seeing it and understanding it firsthand, you don't really understand what your product needs to do.
turns.zh:
没错，我们得把事情彻底弄清楚。比如说，好吧，让我们打开那本大部头的旧教材——如今这些教材都在线版了——看看美国的情况。美国各州和地方政府征收的税种繁多，有的州甚至按城市或县级征收税款。仔细研究其中几个案例就会发现，天哪，我们该如何应对这种未经公告就擅自调整税率的情况？某个城市的行政官员或立法机构决定提高税率，那我们该如何得知这一消息？如何及时调整税率？（00:36:14）  
直到你深入了解这些实际运作方式、沟通流程和深层考量时，才会意识到这些细节的重要性。无论是技术问题、设计难题，还是合规监管或政府事务方面的挑战，任何细节都存在于幕后。除非亲自深入研究并掌握第一手资料，否则你永远无法真正理解产品需要应对的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think an important element of this that's between the lines maybe is don't delegate this to someone. You may have a tax expert on the team, and I imagine many leaders would be like, go figure this out and tell me. And I think what you're saying is you go do that and learn, become the world expert at it.
turns.zh: 我认为其中的核心要义或许在于：别把这类事务外包给别人。团队里或许有税务专家，但很多领导者可能期望他们独立研究并汇报结果。但你的观点是，必须亲自参与学习，成为这方面的专家。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: That's right. That's right. You go do it. You go learn and then we can make the case for hiring the tax expert, which we do have by the way now. That's an incredibly important part of our success is having that specialist but not before somebody with a product mindset. The tax specialist is amazing at tax, right? That's what they're, they love and that's what they do, but that doesn't make them necessarily a great product thinker. So the person with the product thing has to get into those same weeds first to really understand it.
turns.zh: 没错，必须亲自行动。先深入研究，再考虑是否需要聘请税务专家。顺便说一句，我们现在确实有这样的专家了。但这绝不是成功的必要条件，必须先有具备产品思维的人才行。税务专家固然精通税务，但这并不能让他们成为出色的产品思考者。产品团队中的成员必须先深入研究这些复杂细节，才能真正理解全局。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you give any guidance and just how much time to spend on all that stuff versus the regular day-to-day of, say, a product leader on a team, it takes a lot of time to become a world expert on the tax systems of many countries, or is it just there's nothing more important than that, that is your job, and what are you doing not doing that? How do you think about it?
turns.zh: 你是否会提供指导？相较于产品负责人的日常工作，投入多少时间研究这些复杂问题呢？要成为多个国家税务系统的专家，需要耗费大量精力。难道这不比其他任何事情都重要吗？毕竟这是你的职责所在，而你现在却没有做到？你该如何看待这个问题？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think it's equally if a job is 80 hours a week, it's 40 of your hours. I think that you can't really understand a product unless you've gone there. Right? And yes, it takes time and you're right, you can't just ignore the other half of the job of communicating with the engineering team and writing documents or whatever, but what's the point of writing a document if you don't know what you're talking about? And so we very deeply value that. And it's one of the reasons that we keep, at least at Rippling, our product organization really thin. We expect a single leader to be able to know the full scope of the product. In fact, great product leaders can in fact do that because they have this native curiosity and interest and ability to absorb a lot of stuff. And it makes, it's a lot of fun because now I have a group of people around me who are all really good at what they do and really understand what they do and that's kind of just an amazing place to be.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果一份工作每周需要80小时，你得投入其中的40小时才行。我认为除非亲自到现场，否则你根本无法真正理解一款产品。是吧？没错，这确实需要时间，你说得对，你不能忽视与工程团队沟通、撰写文档等另一半工作。但如果你连自己在说什么都不清楚，又怎么能写出有价值的文档呢？因此我们非常重视这一点。这也是我们在Rippling至少保持产品组织精简的原因。我们期望一位领导者能够全面掌控产品全局。事实上，优秀的产品领导者确实能做到这一点，因为他们天生就具有好奇心、兴趣和吸收大量信息的能力。这真的很有趣，现在我身边有一群人，他们都非常擅长自己的工作，深谙其道，这真是个绝佳的团队环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm looking at this list and I just want to keep asking questions about it. One of the sure principles that I love is it reminds me of Amazon has the same principle I believe, which is leaders are right a lot.
turns.zh: 我正在看这份清单，我只想不断追问相关问题。有一个我深爱的核心原则，这让我想起亚马逊也有同样的理念——领导者往往是正确的。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why do you find that to be important? I know you weren't necessarily design all these principles, but I imagine that something that you guys follow often and comes up a lot.
turns.zh: 你为什么觉得这很重要？我知道这些原则不一定都是你制定的，但我想这肯定是你们团队经常遵循且频繁提及的。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I mean, this is one of my favorite ones because I think particularly for a product org, right? Because product leaders have to be right most of the time because their decisions reflect across the entire org and their decisions fundamentally spend time and they spend energy. And if they make good ones, the company does really well. And if they make bad ones, the company doesn't. And one of the things I really value in product leaders are people who can go into an ambiguous information with ambiguous situation, with incomplete information and a complex decision space and can look at that and listen to everybody and read whatever they need to read and say, this is where we need to go. (00:39:43): And even if everyone else is like, ah, I don't know, that feels wrong for this reason, this reason if they have the confidence to make that call, and then a year later when you look back on it, for them to have been right, that's extremely valuable. And it's one of these things that it's really hard to test for. You can get it by talking with people and asking, "Hey, was this person usually right in respect?" And people think about it, but in the context of a given company, just you have to take the time and see if those decisions are largely right. And it's the one value we have. It's like you can't really learn it. Either you're really, really good at making those kinds of decisions or you're not, right? It's a very peculiar skill that we really value.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这是我最喜欢的原则之一，因为我认为这对产品团队来说尤其重要。产品领导者必须大多数时候做对决策，因为他们的决策会影响整个团队，决策本身也耗费大量时间和精力。决策正确，公司就能蓬勃发展；决策失误，公司就会受挫。我非常看重产品领导者能够在模糊的信息、复杂的局面、缺失的数据和艰难的决策环境中，通过倾听各方意见、阅读必要资料，最终判断出正确方向的能力。（00:39:43）即使其他人都说"啊，我不知道"、"这感觉不对"，他们也要有信心做出决定。一年后回头看，如果证明决策正确，这才是最宝贵的价值。这也是很难验证的能力。通过与人交谈，询问"这位领导者通常决策是否正确"，人们会思考这个问题，但在特定公司的语境下，必须花时间观察这些决策是否大体正确。这是我们珍视的价值之一。你无法真正学会这项技能。要么你非常擅长做这类决策，要么不擅长，对吧？这是一项我们非常珍视的独特技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Shifting a little bit, I know you all are going through this global expansion. We talked about this a little bit.
turns.zh: 太棒了。稍微转换一下话题，我知道你们正在进行全球扩张。我们之前也聊过这个。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so just a few questions along this lines, because a lot of companies start one country, most companies do, and then they decide let's expand to new markets. So I guess first question is just how do you decide which markets to go after? And specifically where to start first and then just prioritizing the list of markets? What's kind of your algorithm for that?
turns.zh: 接下来，我想就此提几个问题。很多公司都是从一个国家起步的，而后决定向新市场扩张。所以我的第一个问题是，你们是如何确定拓展目标市场的？具体来说，如何确定首个开拓的市场，以及如何对市场列表进行优先排序？你们的决策算法是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: So it starts with an assumption that we're going to have to be everywhere ultimately, that you don't actually have to build native global payroll in every country in the world. Just makes sense to do that every country in the world. But you definitely want to be able to pay people in any country in the world and you want to be able to have contractors anywhere in the world and have their information be in your HRS anywhere in the world. And so the decision for us, we were fortunate to, or when we made that decision, to have quite a few customers already, like thousands of customers. And so we knew not only where their kind of US employees were, but by virtue of being an employee system work, we actually knew where they had other employees. And so it was quite easy for us to say, focusing on US-based companies, which is incomplete data. (00:41:35): But if we just look at our US-based companies, we know that there is immediate demand for those people to pay people in countries X, Y, and Z. And we just listed those out in raw numerical order. And then we kind of looked at, okay, how hard is it to build in these countries and how valuable is it to build in these countries? What is the strategic value of building in the UK or Canada or Germany or India or wherever? And then we had a discussion on where is there risk or where is this hard? Where is there a long pull? Where does this like, in what countries does it take a long time to get approval or whatever? And we just stack-ranked them and then we revisited that decision. The early decisions that we made on exactly which countries. We have subsequently reordered those over time. And as we've dove, dived in the countries, and learned more, we rejigger things like a little bit. But for the most part, that same basic list we started with is still mostly right.
turns.zh:
首先，我们假设最终要实现全球化布局，但没必要在全球每个国家都建立本地化的薪资系统。合理的做法是在全球多个国家提供薪资支付服务，确保员工无论身处何地都能获得薪资，同时让全球各地的合同工都能在HRS系统中登记信息。对于我们而言，幸运的是做出这一决策时已拥有数千名客户。因此，我们不仅清楚美国员工的分布情况，还能通过员工管理系统掌握其他国家员工的信息。因此，我们决定以美国本土企业为核心开展市场布局（虽然数据不完整）。
（00:41:35）：以美国本土企业为例，我们发现客户对在X、Y、Z等国家支付员工薪资的需求迫切。我们按数字顺序列出这些国家，随后评估在这些国家开展业务的难易度和战略价值。比如，英国、加拿大、德国和印度等市场是否值得开拓？哪些国家存在监管障碍或审批周期过长等挑战？最后，我们对这些国家进行优先排序，并根据后续实践动态调整策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then the other question a lot of founders always struggle with is when is the time to start expanding internationally? Because there's pros and cons. Do you have a sense of what convinced y'all to start going international?
turns.zh: 好的。另一个令许多创始人头疼的问题是，何时该启动国际化扩张？这里面有利有弊。你们是如何下定决心走出国门的？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think our case is slightly special, but I think the right answer to that question is always before you think you do before you think you need to because there are, it's harder than everyone if they've never done it before, it's harder than you think it is. It's more specialized than you think it is. People in the UK really, really care if there is a U in color, just as we care if there's not a U in color. There's just all of these subtle lessons that, like cultural lessons for companies that take a really, really long time to absorb. And so my view is you always should do it earlier than you think you should that, than you think you have to. In our case, it was always something we knew we had to do. In fact, we have a very clear thesis that companies that aren't global, particularly in payroll, but also in kind of insurance and benefits in IT. If you're not global, you're just not going to be around in 10 years because companies were becoming global, and then COVID happened and companies became global much faster. (00:43:35): It stopped being the province of 100-person companies plus and started filtering down into very, very small companies. It just became commonplace for small companies to be multi-country. And so that very much accelerated our timetable. And then you saw other people noticed that too, and you saw other companies starting to try to address parts of this problem as well. And so there's this kind of competitive dimension, which is sort of secondary in most ways because we were going to do it anyway, but that also kind of adds a little bit of a fire under the thing.
turns.zh: 我认为我们的情况略显特殊，但我认为回答这个问题时，永远要先考虑“你以为你懂了”，再考虑“你以为你需要”，因为这比大多数人想象的要难得多。如果你从未做过这件事，那就更难了。它比你想象的要专业得多。英国人真的非常在意“color”里有没有“U”，就像我们在意“color”里有没有“U”一样。还有许多细微的文化差异，比如针对公司的文化教训，这些都需要很长时间才能真正领会。所以我的观点是，你应该比你认为必要的更早行动，比你认为必须的更早行动。在我们案例中，我们一直知道必须这么做。事实上，我们有一个非常明确的论点：那些不走向全球化的公司，特别是在薪资、保险和福利等领域的公司，如果不走向全球化，就无法在未来10年内存续下去。因为公司原本在走向全球化，后来新冠疫情爆发加速了这一进程。（00:43:35）：这不再是只有100人以上大公司的专属领域，已逐渐渗透到非常小的公司。跨国业务对小公司来说已变得司空见惯。这极大地加快了我们的进程。随后其他人也注意到了这一点，其他公司也开始尝试解决部分相关问题。因此存在一种竞争维度，不过在大多数情况下这只是次要的，因为我们无论如何都会这么做，但这也为整个事情增添了一丝紧迫感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What have you found to be most surprising about expanding internationally to be successful in expansion? For folks that are maybe starting down this road of like, oh shoot, we should think about that.
turns.zh: 在向国际扩张以取得成功的过程中，哪些方面最令你感到惊讶？对于那些可能刚刚踏上这条路的人来说，比如“哎呀，我们应该考虑一下这个问题”。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think the thing that was most surprising to me the first time I did this back at Guidewire in the [inaudible 00:44:23] and remains the most surprising thing to most people every time I do this again, is that every country is unique. You can't just take your US-based approach and drop it into another country. Other countries find it insulting. It doesn't matter how much success you've had here. Everyone always believes rightly or wrongly that their local context is special. And you have to respect that. And it comes down to little things like they're being a you in color or not. Or if you ever see a demo delivered to somebody in another country where they see a detailed screen about a person and it includes a social security number, it's like that you immediately lose credibility. Doesn't matter how good all the rest of your stuff is. (00:45:08): And I think that that is consistently the thing that I think is most surprising to people is the degree to which that's true, which seems obvious in retrospect. If you took a German system or something and demoed it in the United States with poorly translated stuff, we would think it would suck too. But it's not, it's really hard to adapt to that mindset. And so it takes just a lot of energy to overcome that organizationally.
turns.zh: 我认为最让我惊讶的是，我第一次在Guidewire做这件事时（[00:44:23的录音不清]），至今每次再做这件事时，最令大多数人惊讶的，就是每个国家都是独特的。你不能简单地把你在美国的做法照搬到其他国家。其他国家会觉得这很无礼。无论你在这里取得了多大的成功都无关紧要。每个人都会或对或错地认为当地的环境是特殊的。你必须尊重这一点。这归结于一些小细节，比如他们是否在颜色里用了正确的你，或者没有。如果你曾向其他国家的人演示某个产品，而他们看到一个详细的个人页面，其中包含社会安全号码，那你立刻就会失去信誉。无论你的其他部分有多好，这都不重要。（00:45:08）：我认为这始终是人们最惊讶的事情，就是这种程度的真实性，现在回想起来似乎很明显。如果你把一个德国系统带到美国演示，翻译得不好，大家也会觉得很糟糕。但事实并非如此，要适应这种思维模式真的很难。因此，在组织层面克服这种困难需要耗费大量精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes tons of sense. I'm going to go in a different direction now.
turns.zh: 很有道理。我现在要转换一下话题。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Frameworks. So I know that you're not a huge fan of frameworks. We were chatting about this before we started recording. And so I'm curious just to hear your perspective on why you're maybe not a fan of frameworks and then also just how you crystallize processes and concepts for your team if you're not just like, Hey, here's our framework you should use.
turns.zh: 框架。嗯，我知道你对框架不是很感冒。我们在开始录制前聊过这个话题。所以我很好奇，想听听你为什么不喜欢框架，以及如果不直接说“嘿，我们用这个框架吧”，你是如何为团队凝练流程和概念的。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Look, I think frameworks are very helpful. So I'm not exactly anti-framework, but I am anti-process as a substitution for deep product thinking, right? So I like to have just enough process to create a frame so that the right decisions can happen and know more. And I think there's a danger, especially as companies scale, that you end up saying, well, if only we categorize everything correctly and Jira, like we will be able to make really good prioritization decisions. So I'm like, sure, extremely helpful to have clear categorization and things that Jira doesn't have like data and analysis and to be able to do all of that stuff. But what you really need to do is decide important to build and then have a way to build it really efficiently. And so I think the right answer, the right amount of process for any given team is like, or the right framework for any team is really just dependent on their specific life cycle. (00:46:47): So you won't see me saying like, oh, we need to use this scrum thing or that combine thing, or whatever the latest, newest thing is. It's like, don't care about any of that. What I care is about something that's going to enable this team in this context at this point in their life cycle to build the right thing as efficiently as possible. And I'm fine if those are different for different teams. And the only place I care about unification is one on the quarterly planning process. And two, everything does need in fact to be in Jira because otherwise, you can't rationalize about what's actually getting done in not.
turns.zh: 听着，我觉得框架确实很有用。说实话，我并不反对框架，但我反对把流程当作深度产品思维的替代品，对吧？所以我认为只需要足够的流程来搭建框架，这样才能做出正确的决策和获取更多信息。特别是随着公司规模扩大，可能会出现这样的危险：你觉得只要把一切都正确分类，放进Jira系统，就能做出高效的优先级排序决策了。但我觉得这其实很危险，尤其是当公司规模扩大后，你可能会想，哦，只要我们把一切都正确分类，再加上Jira系统里没有的数据分析功能，就能做出高效的优先级排序决策了。但你真正需要做的，是决定要构建什么重要的东西，然后高效地构建它。所以我认为任何团队的正确流程或框架，都取决于他们的特定生命周期。（00:46:47）所以你不会看到我说什么，哦，我们要用Scrum框架或者Combine框架，或者其他最新、最热门的东西。我根本不在乎这些。我在乎的是能让团队在当前生命周期中高效构建正确产品的工具。即使不同团队的需求不同，我也无所谓。唯一我关注统一的地方，是季度规划流程。还有，所有数据确实都需要在Jira系统里，因为不然你就无法合理评估实际完成了什么工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a process or framework that you find is counterproductive that you're just stay away from this thing? We've had a lot of trouble with it, or generally, it's like let's just rethink everything ourselves.
turns.zh: 有没有你觉得反生产力的流程或框架，你会直接避开的？我们在很多这类事情上遇到过麻烦，或者通常来说，我们会选择自己重新思考一切。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: No, I don't find one to be particular, I don't consistently found one to be particularly problematic. So I think any framework sort of has its place, the right place, right time. I think there's danger any one time somebody like dogmatically says, I think we should use process X because that's almost never the right answer in my experience. I think there are places where that can differ. Like you start a company on the basis of process X and everyone's bought into that process and everyone understands it. I think they can be really, really great. And on the engineering side, I think this is hugely valuable. It's like test driven-development, first line of code's going to be a test, not the actual thing. Like fantastic, very supportive of all that. I think it's kind of different in the product world.
turns.zh: 不，我没有特别反感的框架，也没有一直觉得特别有问题的。所以我认为任何框架都有它的适用场景、适用时机和适用方式。我觉得只要有人教条式地说，我们应该用X流程，这在我看来几乎从来都不是正确的答案。但不同情况下可能有所不同。比如你基于X流程创立一家公司，所有人都认同这个流程，都理解它。我觉得这时候它可能非常棒。在工程领域，我认为这极具价值。比如测试驱动开发，第一行代码就是测试，而不是实际功能。这太棒了，非常支持这类做法。但在产品领域情况有所不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you had to compare the way Coinbase builds product process-wise or just product development to Rippling, what would you say are the bigger differences?
turns.zh: 如果你要比较Coinbase和Rippling在产品构建流程或产品开发方面的差异，你觉得最大的不同是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think the differences are largely born of the different domains. So crypto, as we talked about earlier, really hard to predict what's going on. There's all these questions about what's the future of crypto, what's going to matter, what do we even need to build? What's going to survive? And so the process we had at Coinbase run, having those debates and getting to a decision and disagreeing, committing. And then from an execution point of view, being able to move fast. That was the trick at Coinbase. Here we know the things that we need to build at a high level. And the trick is how do we really differentiate it on the basis of these amazing platform capabilities we have? Or how do we have to evolve those platform capabilities in order to continue to build something that's just discontinuously better than everything that's out there? And that yields a different decision-making process. So for me, it's the mental model is actually of how I approach those things with the same, but they just yield different results in the actual making of the software.
turns.zh: 我认为这些差异很大程度上源于不同领域的特性。比如加密货币领域，正如我们之前讨论的，其发展极难预测。人们普遍困惑于加密货币的未来走向、哪些要素至关重要、我们究竟需要构建什么产品、哪些项目能存续下去。因此，在Coinbase，我们会开展激烈的辩论，最终达成决策并承受分歧。然后从执行层面来说，关键在于快速行动。这正是Coinbase的成功秘诀。在这里，我们已经明确了高层的构建目标，核心挑战在于如何基于现有出色的平台能力进行差异化创新，或是如何通过不断迭代这些平台能力来持续打造超越现有标准的优质产品。这就催生了截然不同的决策流程。对我而言，关键在于思维模式的转变——尽管处理问题的本质相同，但实际执行效果却天差地别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is that actual difference? Do you find day-to-day? Is it timeline differences? Is it how quickly, I don't know the way you structure, how far out you plan, what do you find is the concrete difference as a result?
turns.zh: 具体差异体现在何处？您在日常工作中是否能察觉？是时间节点上的差异吗？是决策速度的快慢差异吗？还是规划周期的长短差异？您认为具体的区别体现在哪里？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I think the difference is in the day-to-day velocity of decision-making, because we can, Rippling, if you're on, I don't know, pick a random team. If you're on the device management team, you know what you got to do, right? There's no ambiguity. You're not debating about whether Mac or Windows is going to exist in the future. There's none of that cognitive dissonance. There is, we need to build this. It's hard to figure out how we need to build this, right? Because there's all these different things that we could leverage, but we need to basically get this done. (00:49:58): And so the kind of total velocity I would say is higher here, which does not say people work harder or less are at Columbia. Columbia was an amazingly fast environment, but it was also subject to the fact that you just don't know what the crypto markets are going to do, and you have to be incredibly reactive to that. And so I think maybe that's the one thing, like the reactivity to the environment and the crypto environment, what's going on, and the uncertainty of the regulatory environment, all that stuff. We got really, really, really good at handling those things really rapidly, which is something that we need to handle somewhat less [inaudible 00:50:34].
turns.zh: 我认为差异在于日常决策的速度。举个例子，假设你随机挑选一个团队，比如设备管理团队。成员们清楚自己的职责，没有认知偏差，不需要纠结于Mac和Windows系统在未来是否会共存。没有这种认知矛盾，只需专注于如何完成当前任务。（00:49:58）：所以我认为这里整体的决策速度更快，这并不意味着哥伦比亚大学的团队更努力或更不努力。哥伦比亚大学的环境确实非常高效，但也受限于加密货币市场的不可预测性，我们必须对此保持高度敏感。因此，我认为关键在于对市场环境和监管环境的不确定性做出快速反应。正是在这种高压环境下，我们练就了快速应对的能力，而现在我们只需要稍微降低这种压力即可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds quite stressful at Coinbase.
turns.zh: 在Coinbase工作压力很大。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah, I mean it was fun. Yes, it was stressful. I mean, every job I've ever had has been stressful, but in its own unique way. But all of that stress I think is in the shape of a problem, that's in the context of a problem that's really interesting. I mean that's why I stayed at these places. But yeah, it's stressful.
turns.zh: 是的，但也乐在其中。没错，压力很大。但我从事过的每一份工作都有压力，只是方式各不相同。但所有这些压力都源于一个有趣的问题情境，这也是我留在这些公司的根本原因。不过确实很有压力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And looking back, what a joy.
turns.zh: 回首往事，那段时光真是美妙。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah. No, there are very good memories. I look back, I don't really, I remember the stress, but I don't like re-experience it, right. I remember foraging these relationships and building these amazing products that I've been so lucky to be a part of. And so I have almost only good memories of the places I've been.
turns.zh: 是的。确实有很多美好的回忆。回想起来，虽然记得当时的压力，但并不想重温那种焦虑感。记得与同事建立深厚的情谊，参与打造那些令人惊叹的产品，能参与其中真是我的幸运。所以对曾待过的公司，我几乎只有美好的回忆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I find too. You go through these hardships and then you look back and you're like, wow, that was so cool. But assuming they go well, assuming the company works out and-
turns.zh: 我也这么觉得。你经历这些艰难时刻后，回头看会感叹，哇，那真是太棒了。但假设一切顺利，公司发展顺利的话——

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... it feels like it was successful. A lot of times you're at a startup, your life sucks for two years and it doesn't work out and that there is a lot of upside and good memories to that, but it's less glorious.
turns.zh: ……感觉就像成功了。很多时候在初创公司，你会经历两年的艰难时光，最后公司失败了，但其中也有很多积极的方面和美好的回忆，只是没那么光彩。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah, that's fair though. I mean, the first company I was really at out of school's company called Reactivity back in internet one era, and we were trying to figure out how does this internet thing work and how do we start companies on the basis of these tech new technologies and how do we help other companies build stuff and figure it out? And that company fundamentally didn't work out, ultimately got kind of spun itself out and got acquired, which was great, but it was this extraordinary set of people that I was so lucky to work with and I loved all the time I spent there and it was foundational to everything else I ever did. And so even though that effort didn't pay off in the traditional set, the value of the learnings I had there and then the people I had a chance to work with was just really exceptional. So I feel very lucky.
turns.zh: 是啊，这也挺公平的。我的意思是，我毕业后加入的第一家公司是Reactivity，属于互联网1.0时代。我们当时试图弄清楚互联网是如何运作的，如何基于新兴技术创办公司，以及如何帮助其他公司开发产品和解决难题。但那家公司最终没能成功，最后被拆分并被收购，虽然结果不错，但与那些优秀的团队共事的时光让我倍感幸运，我在那里的每一天都无比珍贵，这段经历为我后续的所有工作奠定了基础。所以尽管这次创业没有获得传统意义上的成功，但我在那里学到的知识和结交的伙伴都非常宝贵。我觉得自己很幸运。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good point actually. And I think I should correct even what I said that even when things don't work out, traditionally those experiences end up being incredibly valuable in all these unexpected ways.
turns.zh: 这确实是个很棒的观点。甚至我觉得我之前的表述有误，即便事情没有成功，传统意义上的这些经历最终也会以各种意想不到的方式带来极大的价值。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah, 100%.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay, so final topic.
turns.zh: 好的，最后一个话题。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about hiring product managers and interviewing.
turns.zh: 我想谈谈招聘产品经理和面试相关的话题。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you've hired a lot of PMs over the years. I'm curious, what's something you've learned about what to look for in product managers and also just in product leaders that other people may not be focused on as enough?
turns.zh: 这些年你招聘了不少产品经理。我很好奇，在寻找产品经理以及产品负责人时，你有什么特别的收获，而其他人可能没有足够重视的方面？

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I mean, I don't know that I have any particularly special insight here. I think there's a couple things that I do ask that maybe are more of an emphasis because it's Rippling than not. But the first of those is when people are going through our process, there's a part where they do this case study and an important part of the case study is that it's actually too complex for people to have all of the answers upfront. There's just the space of the problem is too large to do that, which means that in the interview there's a lot of opportunities or in the case study there's a lot of opportunities. So just ask ad hoc questions or to change one assumption. And seeing how people react to that is really indicative of how deeply they understand a new problem or how quickly or how mentally agile they are. (00:53:47): And some people are extremely good at that here in assumption and they blink a couple times. They're like, oh, well that has these 400 implications. And they just start rattling them off. And some people get really flummoxed. I mean obviously for our environment, that former is really, really important to us. I think the other thing that really matters to me is the insightfulness of questions that people ask, which is indicative of number one, their actual interest in the job. (00:54:14): People tend to ask better questions when they're more excited about working at a place and done their research and are asking people about it. And also the quality of those questions can vary quite dramatically. And that's okay. I don't expect the quality to be the same all the time, but sometimes people ask a question, I'm like, "Oh man, I would've never thought to ask that question. That's such an insightful question." And then I pause and I have to think about my answer a little bit. And so it kind of pushes me to be a little bit better. And when that happens, I know I usually have pretty good candidate on my hands.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我不知道自己在这里有没有什么特别独到的见解。我认为有几个问题是我特别强调的，因为这与Rippling的理念息息相关。但首先，当人们经历我们的招聘流程时，会有一个案例研究环节，而案例研究中最重要的一点是，问题的复杂度超出了人们能提前准备好所有答案的范畴。问题的维度实在太大了，这意味着在面试中或案例研究中有很多机会。比如，你可以随口提问，或者改变某个假设。观察人们对此的反应，能很好地反映出他们对新问题的理解深度，以及他们的思维敏捷度和反应速度。（00:53:47）：有些人在假设变更方面非常擅长。他们会快速思考出400种可能的影响。还有些人则完全被难住了。显然，对于我们的团队来说，前者对我们来说非常重要。我认为另一个对我来说很重要的是人们提问的洞察力，这首先反映了他们对这份工作的真正兴趣。（00:54:14）：当人们对在某个公司工作更感兴趣、做了充分调研并向面试官提问时，他们往往会提出更好的问题。而这些问题的质量差异巨大。这没关系。我不期望问题质量始终如一，但有时人们会问一个问题，我会想：“哇，我从没想过要这么问。这真是个有洞察力的问题。”然后我得停下来好好思考答案。这会促使我不断提升自己。当这种情况发生时，我知道我面前通常是个很优秀的候选人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of someone asking a really good question that comes to mind that you think back to and like, Oh wow, that was great.
turns.zh: 你能想到有人问过一个非常好的问题，让你回想起来会说，哇，真棒。

turns.speaker: Jeremy Henrickson
turns.en: I remember about three years ago I was interviewing a guy named Kyle Boston and Kyle is now runs our platform product organization. And I can't remember the specific question he asked, but it had something to do with, wait a minute, if you have all these products and you have this employee system of record thing underneath it, we be thinking about how to create these various pillars of underlying platform technology, things like [inaudible 00:55:22] all this stuff. And this was before we fully formalized the concept of our platform beyond the kind of employee system of record. (00:55:29): And I remember thinking, yes, we should, and that had entered our minds before, but the fact that somebody which who had almost no context on the company, that's what was impressive about this question. It's like, man, you've been thinking about Rippling for a couple weeks while you're interviewing with a bunch of other companies or whatever. And you've thought about it deeply enough to have this insight into the nature of the platform that we're building immediately gave me a bunch of confidence in his ability to think through the sorts of things we need him to think through.
turns.zh: 我记得大约三年前，我面试了一个叫凯尔·波士顿的人，他现在负责我们的平台产品部门。我不记得他具体问了什么问题，但问题与此有关：等等，如果你有这么多产品，又有员工系统记录底层架构，我们该如何构建底层平台技术的各个支柱，比如[00:55:22未听清]所有这些东西。这是在我们将平台概念正式化为员工系统记录之外的阶段之前。（00:55:29）：我记得当时我想，是的，我们应该这么做，这个想法我们之前也有过，但有人几乎对公司没有背景信息，却能提出这个问题，这太令人印象深刻了。这就像，伙计，你在面试其他公司或做其他事情的同时，已经思考Rippling好几周了。而你能如此深入地思考我们正在构建的平台的本质，这让我对他的思维能力充满信心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
